However, its integration with Nature-Inspired Algorithms (NIAs) remains fragmented, with limited understanding of strategies, challenges, and outcomes. This paper presents the first systematic review focused exclusively on the use of TL in NIAs, excluding deep learning approaches. Major challenges include dealing with domain/ task similarity, avoiding negative transfer, selecting what and when to transfer, and adapt- ing TL mechanisms to population-based search paradigms. This review provides a foundation for researchers interested in designing adaptive, efficient, and knowledge-guided metaheuristics for complex optimization tasks. Xavier, L. N. de Castro 1 Introduction The increasing complexity of optimization problems in real-world applications has driven the development of adaptive and intelligent computational techniques. Among these, nature- inspired algorithms (NIAs) have gained prominence due to their flexibility, scalability, and ability to operate in dynamic, high-dimensional environments. At the same time, transfer learning (TL) has emerged as a promising approach to enhance learning systems by reusing knowledge across tasks and domains. Combining these two paradigms opens new oppor- tunities to solve challenging problems more efficiently and with stronger generalization capabilities. 1.1 Motivation and problem statement Natural Computing (NC) studies and models natural processes and phenomena to develop nature-inspired algorithms that solve problems inadequately addressed by traditional methods. Nature-inspired algorithms, such as Evolutionary Algorithms (EA) and Swarm Intelligence (SI), illustrate how understanding the behavior of living organisms–whether collectively or individually–can inspire technological and scientific advances De Castro (2006). NC algorithms have been successfully applied not only to computational tasks such as image and document classification but also to industrial systems Ardeh et al. (2021), logistics problems Zheng et al. (2022), and manufacturing processes Zhou et al. (2023). NC systems are capable of adapting to their operating environments. For example, Genetic Algorithms (GA) evolve populations through genetic variation, while Particle Swarm Optimization (PSO) algorithms allow individuals to adjust their behavior based on social interactions Siddique and Adeli (2015). This adaptability is a key feature that makes nature-inspired algorithms suitable for complex, dynamic problems. Transfer Learning (TL), in turn, enables knowledge from a model trained on one task or domain (source) to be reused to accelerate learning or improve performance on another task or domain (target) Pan and Yang (2009). Although widely used in deep learning, TL holds promising potential in other paradigms, including nature-inspired algorithms. This relevance is particularly clear in optimization contexts, where understanding why knowl- edge transfer improves convergence and generalization is just as important as designing the transfer mechanism itself. By integrating TL into NIAs, it is possible to improve generalization, reduce learning time, and decrease computational costs. For example, an Ant Colony Optimization (ACO) algorithm could benefit from reusing a previously learned pheromone map instead of recon- structing it from scratch at every iteration Singh and Pillay (2022). Although transfer learning is well established in deep learning contexts, its application in NIAs remains underexplored. Existing reviews mostly focus on neural networks, overlook- ing adaptations required for TL in evolutionary and swarm-based algorithms. To the best of our knowledge, no prior systematic review has specifically investigated the intersection of TL and NIAs outside of deep learning. This work addresses that gap by analyzing the main strategies, objectives, and challenges involved in this integration. The motivation behind this review stems from the increasing complexity of real-world optimization problems and the need for more efficient, generalizable, and adaptive meta- heuristics. While nature-inspired algorithms are robust, they often suffer from high compu- 1 3 On the use of transfer learning in nature-inspired algorithms: a… Page 3 of 34 22 tational costs, limited re-usability, and sensitivity to initial configurations. Transfer learning presents an opportunity to overcome these limitations by transferring prior knowledge to new problem settings. Nevertheless, open challenges such as domain/task mismatch, the risk of negative transfer, and the precise definition of transferable components remain cru- cial obstacles to be addressed. The objective of this paper is to conduct a systematic review focused exclusively on the use of Transfer Learning in Nature-Inspired Algorithms (excluding deep learning), intend- ing to identify key strategies, challenges, and research trends that may support the develop- ment of more adaptive and reusable metaheuristics in complex optimization scenarios. Furthermore, this review not only describes existing approaches but also discusses why certain transfer learning strategies tend to be more effective than others when integrated with NIAs. These differences often stem from algorithmic properties, such as adaptability, representation of knowledge, and robustness to dynamic environments, which directly influ- ence transferability and performance gains. 1.2 Contributions This paper makes the following main contributions: ● It presents the first systematic review that exclusively investigates the integration of transfer learning in nature-inspired algorithms, excluding deep learning approaches, thus addressing a specific gap in the literature. ● It proposes a novel classification framework for TL strategies used in NIAs, organiz- ing them based on learning paradigms (inductive, transductive, unsupervised), transfer components (what, when, how), and algorithmic goals. ● It identifies and synthesizes key technical challenges in combining TL with NIAs, such as domain/task mismatch, risk of negative transfer, and difficulties in defining transfer- able components. ● It reveals recurring patterns across 47 primary studies and provides a comparative anal- ysis of how different TL strategies are implemented in evolutionary and swarm-based algorithms. ● It outlines open research directions and future opportunities for designing adaptive and generalizable TL-based metaheuristics in complex optimization scenarios. Feature extraction and representation learning: Extract and represent informative features from data from the source domain, ensuring that these features are relevant and transferable to the source and target tasks. 3. Model adaptation: Adapt the model, often pre-trained on the source task, to the target task, while considering any discrepancies in data distributions and label spaces between the source and target domains. 4. The focus here is on how transfer learning can be employed in the adaptation processes of nature-inspired algorithms to improve their per- formance. There are three main issues to consider before applying a transfer learning solu- tion to an algorithm: “What to transfer?”, “When to transfer?”, and “How to transfer?”, as previously discussed. 1 3 On the use of transfer learning in nature-inspired algorithms: a… Page 15 of 34 22 Regarding “what to transfer?”, the concern lies in understanding which fragment of knowledge can be reused between tasks or domains Pan and Yang (2009). While some knowledge is specific to a particular domain or task, some components may be common to both, which can help improve performance. Identification of these transferable elements is critical to avoid ineffective or counterproductive knowledge transfer. Once transferable knowledge is identified, it is necessary to determine how it will be applied from one domain or task to another. Regarding “when to transfer?”, it is important to investigate under which conditions knowledge transfer should occur. These considerations help prevent negative transfer and ensure that TL strategies are contextually appropriate. It is equally important to identify situations in which knowledge transfer should not be performed. If these aspects are neglected, performance can be compromised, potentially resulting in negative transfer, where knowledge reuse degrades the target task’s outcomes. Empirical evidence demonstrates that if two tasks are very dissimilar, indiscriminate trans- fer can harm the performance of the target tasks Rosenstein et al. (2005). This highlights the necessity of evaluating task and domain similarity prior to TL application in NIAs. Two main groups of Nature-Inspired Algorithms (NIA) were detected as employing transfer learning solutions, totaling 49 articles (base studies). Of these, 42 papers focus on Evolutionary Computing, as shown in Table 4, and 7 are based on Swarm Intelligence, as shown in Table 5. Among the retrieved works, some papers were authored by the same research groups, with six different groups producing multiple works, in addition to groups with only one study on a given topic. While several propos- als focused on adapting transfer mechanisms, few presented robust comparative analyses or ablation studies to validate the effectiveness of the transferred knowledge. The lack of comprehensive validation in real-world contexts limits the generalization of reported results and indicates an important avenue for future research. Regarding "when to transfer?", it is crucial to understand the appropriate timing for the transfer. In DMOEA and SMOEA, strategies include knowledge transfer during pre-search, upon detection of environmental changes, or during the evolutionary process itself (Ye et al. 2022a; Ji et al. 2022; Yao and Wang 2023; Jiang et al. 2017; Zhao et al. 2023; Jiang et al. 2020a; Zhenzhong et al. 2019; Jiang et al. 2020b; Zhang et al. 2023a, b, c, d; He and Ren 2022; Aliniya and Khasteh 2023; Wu et al. 2023; Liu and Wang 2021; Jiang et al. 2020c; Zhenzhong et al. 2020; Wang et al. 2022a). Conversely, MOEA/D, MFEA, and MOEC/D approaches transfer knowledge after each detected change in the dynamic environment, using change detection mechanisms and window size parameters to control the frequency of transfer (Ye et al. 2022b; Lu et al. 2023; Ma et al. 2020; Fan et al. 2020; Liu et al. 2019). GP algorithms perform transfers during the design phase, initialization, or in situations such as label scarcity, adapting the strategy to the algorithm’s specific context (Fu et al. 2019; Iqbal et al. 2019; Chen et al. 2019; Muller et al. 2019; Hu et al. 2023). In GPHH, transfers occur at convergence, before fine-tuning, at the start of each generation, or dur- ing initialization, depending on the algorithm’s objective Ardeh et al. (2021, 2020a, 2020b, 2020c, 2019); Russell and Pillay (2023); Chen et al. (2023). GA, DE, and ES typically transfer knowledge during parallel optimization processes or prior to starting optimization on target problems (Zhang and Wang 2021; Huang et al. 2023; Chen et al. 2021; Lai et al. 2023; Chen and Liu 2021; Chen et al. 2021). Overall, the timing of knowledge transfer is determined by both the algorithm’s design and the characteristics of the problem domain, aiming to minimize negative transfer and maximize efficiency. 4.1.3 How to transfer? As for "how to transfer?", it is necessary to understand the techniques used to perform TL. Generally, each algorithm in the base studies follows a specific strategy, reflecting the diver- sity of techniques within transfer learning and the variety of problems they aim to solve. In some MOEAs, transfer occurs sequentially: from the previous (source) environment to the current one, and then from the current to the next (target) environment (Ye et al. 2022a; Ji et al. 2022; Yao and Wang 2023; Jiang et al. 2017; Zhao et al. 2023; Jiang et al. 2020a; Zhen- zhong et al. 2019; Jiang et al. 2020b; Zhang et al. 2023a, b, c, d; He and Ren 2022; Aliniya and Khasteh 2023; Wu et al. 2023; Liu and Wang 2021; Jiang et al. 2020c; Zhenzhong et al. 2020). This approach leverages the adaptive nature of the algorithms. Other MOEAs aim to minimize the negative effects of transfer by improving feature representation, similarly to MFEA (Ye et al. 2022b; Fan et al. 2020; Wang et al. 2022a; Lu et al. 2023; Ma et al. 2020; Liu et al. 2019). GPHH algorithms use genetic operators like crossover and mutation on selected rout- ing policies, replacing the worst policies with the best newly generated ones (Ardeh et al. 2021, 2020a, b, c, 2019; Russell and Pillay 2023; Chen et al. 2023). DE and ES adopt more dynamic strategies, sharing the best features throughout the evolutionary process (Huang 1 3 22 Page 22 of 34 R. Xavier, L. N. de Castro et al. 2023; Chen et al. 2021; Lai et al. 2023; Chen and Liu 2021; Chen et al. 2021). PSO algorithms demonstrate adaptive dynamic parameter adjustments in variable environments, similar to ACO and ABC algorithms (Zheng et al. 2022; Lu et al. 2023; Huang et al. 2023; Fang et al. 2021; Huang and Chen 2021; Zhou et al. 2023; Singh and Pillay 2022). This diversity of TL strategies–including sequential transfer, feature representation improvement, dynamic sharing, and parameter adaptation–reflects the complexity required to optimize knowledge transfer across different algorithms and problem contexts. 4.2 Goals of TL in nature-inspired algorithms Recent studies have demonstrated a growing interest in applying NIAs to functional and real-world optimization problems. Enhanced PSO variants have been proposed for global optimization Lu et al. (2023), while hybrid approaches such as ACO combined with CNNs have proven effective in medical diagnosis tasks like autism spectrum classification Ashraf et al. (2025). Additionally, algorithm refinements such as the Fire Hawks Optimizer Ashraf et al. (2023) and bat algorithm variants Bangyal et al. (2018) have advanced convergence and solution diversity. Research on mutation strategies in PSO has also contributed to prac- tical applicability Bangyal et al. (2020). These developments emphasize the relevance of improving NIA adaptability and efficiency through TL. When integrated with NIAs, TL enables benefits that surpass conventional optimiza- tion, such as reusing knowledge across tasks, adapting to dynamic problems, and improving solutions in low-data scenarios. These advantages are particularly relevant in real-world applications where data availability and computational resources are limited (Ardeh et al. 2020a, b, c, 2019, 2021). Among the most significant benefits are the ability to reuse knowledge from past tasks to reduce search time; improved adaptability to dynamic and multi-scenario problems; greater efficiency in solving tasks with limited or costly data; and a reduction in the algorithm’s dependency on random initialization. These advantages are especially important in real- world scenarios where resource constraints, data scarcity, or dynamic environments demand fast and adaptive solutions. Understanding how TL is being incorporated into NIAs helps reveal which strategies are more promising and where further innovation is possible (Weiss et al. 2016; Zhuang et al. 2020; Pan and Yang 2009). The analysis cov- ered 47 primary studies, examining how TL has been integrated into evolutionary and swarm-based algorithms across learning paradigms, transfer strategies, algorithmic goals, and problem domains. The results demonstrate that TL can significantly enhance NIAs by improving gener- alization, accelerating convergence, reducing dependency on random initialization, and enabling knowledge reuse in data-scarce or dynamic environments. Key theoretical chal- lenges remain, particularly concerning the core TL questions: what knowledge to transfer, when to transfer, and how to transfer it effectively. Mishandling these aspects may lead to negative transfer, performance degradation, or increased algorithmic complexity. Neverthe- less, diverse strategies have emerged, highlighting the adaptability and interdisciplinary potential of TL in NIA contexts. Practically, TL-enabled NIAs have shown advantages in solving complex problems such as multiobjective, dynamic, and discrete optimization, with growing applications in logistics, manufacturing, and healthcare. However, notable gaps persist, including limited research on clustering and combinatorial tasks, underrepresented unsupervised learning approaches, parameter transfer, and the lack of standardized evaluation protocols. Future research should investigate novel TL mechanisms tailored for NIAs, especially in multitask and unsupervised settings. Emphasis is needed on effective feature transfer, domain adaptation, and hybrid model design. Additionally, integrating TL with underex- plored paradigms, such as artificial immune systems and other bioinspired techniques, rep- resents a promising avenue. 1 3 On the use of transfer learning in nature-inspired algorithms: a… Page 31 of 34 22 This review consolidates current efforts to combine TL with nature-inspired approaches, highlighting significant opportunities for advancement. JSON: Name: adaptive_param_transfer_swarm Title: Adaptive unsupervised parameter and population transfer for swarm-intelligence solvers on dynamic traveling salesman problems Short Hypothesis: An adaptive unsupervised transfer mechanism that transfers both population solutions and algorithm parameters from previous environment states to a swarm-intelligence solver causes a statistically significant reduction in average tour length and convergence time on dynamic traveling salesman problems compared to (a) the same solver without transfer and (b) solvers using instance-only or parameter-only transfer. Related Work: Prior work applies transfer learning to nature-inspired optimizers using three main strategies: instance-transfer (reusing past solutions to seed new searches), feature-representation-transfer (learning shared embeddings or surrogates across tasks), and parameter-transfer (reusing hyperparameters or distribution statistics). Most studies target evolutionary algorithms; swarm-intelligence applications are fewer and focus primarily on instance or feature transfers. Timing strategies are typically fixed (pre-initialization) or triggered by coarse change detection; robust dynamic schedulers are rare. Limitations in existing approaches include: (1) underexplored combined parameter+instance transfer despite complementary benefits; (2) scarce use of unsupervised domain-similarity measures to avoid negative transfer; (3) lack of adaptive, online decision rules for when to transfer; (4) limited evaluations on dynamic combinatorial benchmarks (e.g., TSP variants), and few ablation studies isolating parameter vs instance effects. These gaps motivate a unified adaptive framework that (a) jointly transfers parameters and solutions, (b) uses unsupervised similarity scoring to decide transfers, and (c) evaluates effects across dynamic combinatorial benchmarks. Abstract: Dynamic combinatorial optimization tasks such as the dynamic traveling salesman problem (DTSP) require solvers that adapt rapidly to changing instance structure. Existing transfer-learning interventions for nature-inspired optimizers either reuse past solutions or adapt parameters, but seldom both, and typically rely on static transfer schedules that risk negative transfer when environments diverge. We propose an adaptive unsupervised transfer framework for swarm-intelligence solvers that jointly transfers population-level solutions and algorithm parameters from recent environment states. The framework computes an unsupervised domain-similarity score between past and current states, uses an online change detector to identify transfer opportunities, and applies a dynamic scheduler that decides whether to transfer population members, parameter settings, or both. The primary contributions are: (1) a combined parameter+instance transfer protocol for swarm optimizers, (2) an unsupervised similarity metric and online scheduler to avoid negative transfer, and (3) a comprehensive experimental evaluation on DTSP scenarios. We expect the method to reduce convergence time and average tour length while maintaining robustness across varying degrees of dynamism. Experiments: Datasets: (1) Synthetic dynamic TSP instances created from standard TSP benchmarks by applying controlled city perturbations (relocation, insertion, deletion) at specified change frequencies; dataset sets: small (50 cities), medium (200 cities), large (1000 cities); dynamism levels: low, medium, high (change interval parameters: 5000, 2000, 500 evaluations). (2) Real-world routing traces converted to dynamic sequences (vehicle routing logs segmented into time windows). Baselines: vanilla PSO, vanilla ACO, instance-transfer PSO (seeded with archived best tours), parameter-transfer PSO (transfer only velocity/inertia/cognitive/social parameters), feature-representation transfer method (surrogate-based initial population), and an oracle upper-bound (best-of-source solutions chosen with hindsight). Proposed variants: full joint-transfer (population+parameters with adaptive scheduler), population-only adaptive-transfer, parameter-only adaptive-transfer, fixed-schedule joint-transfer. Evaluation metrics: average tour length (mean over runs), best tour length, normalized gap to static optimum, convergence time to 1% of final tour length, computational overhead (CPU seconds), transfer success rate (fraction of transfers that improve immediate post-transfer best), negative transfer rate (fraction that degrade performance vs no-transfer), and statistical significance (Wilcoxon signed-rank, p<0.05). Experimental setup: population size 100 for PSO/ACO, 30 independent random seeds per instance, fixed evaluation budget per dynamic epoch (e.g., 5000 fitness evaluations), uniform stopping criterion, identical initialization distributions across methods. Ablation studies: (A) full vs population-only vs parameter-only vs fixed-schedule; (B) unsupervised similarity metric ablation: clustering-based distance vs embedding cosine vs raw-statistic distance vs random trigger; (C) sensitivity sweep over similarity threshold and change-detection window size. Report per-instance and aggregated results across sizes and dynamism levels, include convergence curves, boxplots, and pairwise Wilcoxon tests. Risk Factors and Limitations: Negative transfer when past states are dissimilar to current states due to inaccurate similarity scoring; delayed or missed transfers if change detector fails to detect environment shifts; overhead of computing similarity metrics and potential scalability limits on large instances (computational cost may offset gains); transfer of parameter settings that are tied to population size or problem scale may not generalize across instance sizes; evaluation bias from synthetic dynamic scenarios that do not reflect real-world temporal patterns; limited transfer effectiveness on problem variants with structural discontinuities (e.g., large city insertions or deletions); reproducibility risks due to sensitivity to random seeds and implementation details of swarm operators; theoretical limitations in guarantees—no formal bound on worst-case degradation from transfer; potential requirement of hyperparameter tuning (similarity threshold, scheduler parameters) which may be dataset-specific.
